o: Select books whose rating column is NULL, projecting id, title, author, year, ordered by book_id. The key SQL fact: NULL comparisons with = yield NULL (not true), so WHERE rating = NULL matches nothing — you must use IS NULL (or the NULL-safe equality operator).
k: Never write rating = NULL; use rating IS NULL.
Ordering by book_id ascending is part of the specification.

a.i: Direct predicate on the nullable column — the idiomatic and index-friendly way.
s: Select the four required columns from books.
Filter with WHERE rating IS NULL.

c.python:
-- MySQL solution
SELECT book_id, title, author, published_year
FROM books
WHERE rating IS NULL
ORDER BY book_id;
c.cpp:

a.t: O(B) — full scan (or index range scan if a rating index exists).

a.i: MySQL's spaceship operator (rating <=> rating) is true only when rating is non-NULL, so negating it finds unrated books — a portable-in-spirit alternative worth mentioning.
s: Negate the NULL-safe self-comparison of rating.
Project and order identically to Approach 1.

c.python:
-- MySQL solution
SELECT book_id, title, author, published_year
FROM books
WHERE NOT (rating <=> rating)
ORDER BY book_id;

c.javascript:

WHERE NOT (rating <=> rating)
ORDER BY book_id;

a.t: O(B) — same scan shape as Approach 1.

w: Always answer with IS NULL; mention <=> only as trivia. Classic pitfall: rating = NULL or rating <> 4.5 silently excluding NULL rows. Follow-up: count rated vs unrated per publication decade, or coalesce NULL ratings to the average.
